title: How do you optimize AWS costs — use Reserved Instances / Savings Plans for predictable workloads, Spot Instances for fault-tolerant batch jobs, right-size instances using CloudWatch metrics, use S3 lifecycle policies to move old data to cheaper storage tiers (S3-IA → Glacier), turn off dev/test environments at night?

s1_definition.profdef: AWS cost optimization is the practice of reducing spend without harming performance or reliability, using several levers: commit to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for steady, predictable workloads to get large discounts over on-demand; use Spot Instances for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work at up to around ninety percent off; right-size instances by using CloudWatch utilization metrics to match capacity to actual demand; apply S3 lifecycle policies to move aging data to cheaper storage tiers; and shut down non-production environments outside working hours. The goal is to match supply to real demand and pay the lowest appropriate price for each workload.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of running National Bank of India's branches. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are like signing a one or three-year lease on the branches you know you will always need, getting a big discount versus paying daily hotel rates. Spot Instances are like using cheap temporary staff for overflow work you can pause anytime — great for sorting a backlog overnight, but they might be sent home at short notice. Right-sizing is noticing a branch has ten tellers but only ever needs four, and letting the extra six go. S3 lifecycle tiers are moving old files from the expensive front office to a cheap basement archive. And turning off dev/test at night is switching off the lights and air conditioning in the training rooms nobody uses after 7 p.m.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AWS cost optimization is the practice of reducing spend without harming performance or reliability, using several levers: commit to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for steady, predictable workloads to get large discounts over on-demand; use Spot Instances for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work at up to around ninety percent off; right-size instances by using CloudWatch utilization metrics to match capacity to actual demand; apply S3 lifecycle policies to move aging data to cheaper storage tiers; and shut down non-production environments outside working hours. The goal is to match supply to real demand and pay the lowest appropriate price for each workload.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of running National Bank of India's branches. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are like signing a one or three-year lease on the branches you know you will always need, getting a big discount versus paying daily hotel rates. Spot Instances are like using cheap temporary staff for overflow work you can pause anytime — great for sorting a backlog overnight, but they might be sent home at short notice. Right-sizing is noticing a branch has ten tellers but only ever needs four, and letting the extra six go. S3 lifecycle tiers are moving old files from the expensive front office to a cheap basement archive. And turning off dev/test at night is switching off the lights and air conditioning in the training rooms nobody uses after 7 p.m.

**One line to remember:** Cut AWS cost by committing to Savings Plans for steady workloads, Spot for interruptible batch, right-sizing from CloudWatch metrics, S3 lifecycle tiering for old data, and shutting off dev/test when idle.

sections.s2_technical:
The first lever is commitment-based discounts for predictable, always-on workloads. On-demand pricing is the most expensive per hour because it is fully flexible. If a workload runs continuously, I commit to a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances for one or three years and get a large discount, often in the range of up to roughly seventy percent. Savings Plans are generally more flexible than classic Reserved Instances because they apply across instance families and even to Fargate and Lambda for the compute variety.

```java
// Deciding commitment based on steady baseline usage
record UsageProfile(int steadyHoursPerDay, boolean interruptible) {}
UsageProfile ledger = new UsageProfile(24, false); // always-on → commit (Savings Plan)
UsageProfile batch  = new UsageProfile(2,  true);  // interruptible → Spot
```

The second lever is Spot Instances for fault-tolerant, interruptible work. Spot uses spare AWS capacity at up to around ninety percent off on-demand, but AWS can reclaim it with a two-minute warning. So Spot is perfect for batch jobs, data processing, and stateless workers that can be interrupted and resumed, and wrong for a stateful always-on service that cannot tolerate sudden termination.

The third lever is right-sizing using CloudWatch metrics. I look at real CPU, memory, and network utilization over time, and if an instance sits at ten percent CPU, I move it to a smaller instance type, saving money with no performance loss. AWS Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer's rightsizing recommendations automate much of this analysis.

The fourth lever is S3 lifecycle policies. Data that is hot now becomes cold later, so I write lifecycle rules that transition objects from Standard to Standard-IA, then to Glacier, and finally expire them, so I am not paying premium storage rates for data nobody reads.

The fifth lever is shutting down non-production environments outside working hours. Development and test environments usually do not need to run nights and weekends, so a scheduler stops them in the evening and starts them in the morning, which can cut their cost by roughly two-thirds since they only run about a third of the week.

Beyond these, I attribute cost with tagging so each team sees its own spend, set budgets and alerts to catch surprises, delete unattached EBS volumes and idle load balancers, and prefer managed and serverless services that scale to zero for spiky workloads.

A senior nuance: cost optimization is a continuous discipline, not a one-time cleanup, and it must never silently trade away reliability. I combine levers — commit to the steady baseline with a Savings Plan, burst on Spot or on-demand above it, right-size continuously, and tier storage — and I always tie the baseline commitment to a well-understood steady load so I do not over-commit to capacity I will not use.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a mix of workloads: an always-on core ledger, a nightly fraud-analysis batch that can tolerate interruption, oversized web servers running at low CPU, old statement data sitting in expensive storage, and development environments running around the clock. Paying on-demand full price for all of this wastes a large amount of money. This is exactly what applying the right cost lever per workload solves.

Problem 2 — The finance team needs to know the expected saving from each action to prioritize. This is exactly what a cost advisor that estimates savings provides.

We will write a small cost-optimization advisor. `CostItem` describes a resource's usage profile. `CostOptimizer` recommends the right lever (Savings Plan, Spot, right-size, S3 lifecycle, scheduled shutdown) and estimates the relative saving. The demo runs the ledger, the fraud batch, an oversized web server, old S3 data, and a dev environment.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five resources — an always-on core ledger, an interruptible fraud batch, a low-CPU web server, old statement storage, and a round-the-clock development environment.

Step 1. The core ledger is evaluated. It runs twenty-four hours a day, is not interruptible, and is well utilized, so the advisor recommends a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances, estimating up to about seventy percent saving by committing to its steady baseline.

Step 2. The fraud batch is evaluated. It is interruptible and runs only a couple of hours, so the advisor recommends Spot Instances, estimating up to about ninety percent off, because the job can be paused and resumed if AWS reclaims the capacity.

Step 3. The web server is evaluated. It runs all day but its CloudWatch CPU utilization is only ten percent, so the advisor recommends right-sizing it to a smaller instance, estimating around fifty percent saving with no performance loss since the capacity was never used.

Step 4. The old statement storage is evaluated. It is cold storage data, so the advisor recommends an S3 lifecycle policy that moves it from Standard to Standard-IA to Glacier and eventually expires it, giving a large saving by not paying premium rates for unread data.

Step 5. The development environment is evaluated. It is non-production yet runs around the clock, so the advisor recommends scheduling it to shut down nights and weekends, estimating about sixty-five percent saving because it would then run only about a third of the week.

Step 6. The final output logs each resource with its recommended lever and estimated saving, giving finance a prioritized action list.

```
2026-10-29 03:10:00 [INFO] core-ledger -> Savings Plan / Reserved Instances (steady, predictable, up to ~70% off) [est. saving up to ~70% (1-3yr commit)]
2026-10-29 03:10:00 [INFO] fraud-batch -> Spot Instances (fault-tolerant batch, up to ~90% off) [est. saving up to ~90%]
2026-10-29 03:10:00 [INFO] web-server -> Right-size to a smaller instance (low CPU in CloudWatch) [est. saving ~50% (half-size instance)]
2026-10-29 03:10:00 [INFO] old-statements -> S3 lifecycle: Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier → expire [est. saving large (cold tiers vs Standard)]
2026-10-29 03:10:00 [INFO] dev-environment -> Schedule shutdown nights/weekends (runs ~1/3 of the week) [est. saving ~65% (off nights/weekends)]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Resource usage profile → CostOptimizer.recommend()
    │
    ├─ storage? ────────────────→ S3 lifecycle (Standard→IA→Glacier→expire)   [large]
    ├─ non-prod? ───────────────→ schedule off nights/weekends                [~65%]
    ├─ interruptible? ──────────→ Spot Instances                              [~90%]
    ├─ CPU < 20% (CloudWatch)? ─→ right-size smaller instance                 [~50%]
    ├─ steady 20h+/day? ────────→ Savings Plan / Reserved Instances           [~70%]
    └─ else ────────────────────→ on-demand (keep flexible)                   [0%]

  Combine levers: commit baseline (Savings Plan) + burst on Spot/on-demand
                  + right-size continuously + tier storage + tag for visibility
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cost optimization on AWS is about matching supply to real demand and paying the lowest appropriate price for each workload without hurting performance or reliability, and I apply several levers depending on the workload's shape. For steady, predictable, always-on workloads I commit to a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances for one or three years, which trades flexibility for a large discount, often up to around seventy percent off on-demand, and I favor Savings Plans because they apply flexibly across instance families and even to Fargate and Lambda.

For fault-tolerant, interruptible work like batch jobs and stateless processing I use Spot Instances, which run on spare capacity at up to around ninety percent off, accepting that AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning, so I only use them where interruption is safe. For everything running, I right-size continuously using CloudWatch utilization metrics and tools like Compute Optimizer: if an instance sits at ten percent CPU, I move it to a smaller type and save money with no performance loss. For storage, I apply S3 lifecycle policies that move aging data from Standard to Standard-IA to Glacier and finally expire it, so I am not paying premium rates for data nobody reads. And for non-production environments, I schedule them to shut down nights and weekends, which cuts their cost by roughly two-thirds because they only run about a third of the week.

On top of those, I tag resources so each team sees its own spend, set budgets and alerts to catch surprises early, and clean up waste like unattached EBS volumes and idle load balancers. The senior point I always make is that cost optimization is a continuous discipline, not a one-time cleanup, and it must never silently trade away reliability — I commit to a well-understood steady baseline, burst above it on Spot or on-demand, and keep right-sizing as usage changes.

At National Bank of India I applied exactly this mix. The always-on core ledger went onto a Savings Plan for its steady baseline, the nightly fraud-analysis batch ran on Spot because it tolerates interruption, and I right-sized a fleet of web servers that CloudWatch showed running at ten percent CPU, halving their cost. Old statement data moved through S3 lifecycle tiers into Glacier, and I scheduled the development and test environments to switch off every evening and weekend. Together these cut our monthly bill substantially, and because I tied each action to measured usage and kept production reliability untouched, none of the savings came at the expense of the customer experience.
